q: Lark Manufacturing had beginning raw materials of $40,000, raw materials purchases of $210,000, and ending raw materials of $30,000. Direct labor was $180,000 and manufacturing overhead was $150,000. Work-in-process inventory was $60,000 at the beginning of the year and $70,000 at year-end. What was Lark's cost of goods manufactured?
exp: Materials used = $40,000 + $210,000 - $30,000 = $220,000; total manufacturing costs = $220,000 + $180,000 + $150,000 = $550,000; COGM = $550,000 + $60,000 - $70,000 = $540,000. Stopping at total manufacturing costs ($550,000) ignores the change in work in process.

q: Mertz Co. incurred direct materials of $220,000, direct labor of $180,000, and manufacturing overhead of $150,000 during the period. What were Mertz's conversion costs?
exp: Conversion costs = direct labor + manufacturing overhead = $180,000 + $150,000 = $330,000. The $400,000 amount is prime cost (direct materials + direct labor).

q: Norris Co. applies overhead on direct labor hours. At the start of the year it estimated overhead of $480,000 and 60,000 direct labor hours. Actual direct labor hours were 62,000 and actual overhead was $505,000. What was Norris's over- or underapplied overhead?
exp: Rate = $480,000 / 60,000 = $8 per hour; applied = 62,000 x $8 = $496,000; actual $505,000 exceeds applied, so overhead is underapplied by $9,000. Comparing actual to budgeted overhead ($25,000) uses the wrong benchmark.

q: Osler Corp. has $30,000 of underapplied overhead at year-end, which it prorates based on the overhead applied in ending balances: 20% in work in process, 30% in finished goods, and 50% in cost of goods sold. What is the effect of the proration on cost of goods sold?
exp: Underapplied overhead means too little cost was charged, so COGS increases by 50% x $30,000 = $15,000. Closing the full $30,000 to COGS ignores the proration, and a decrease would apply to overapplied overhead.

q: Pruitt Co. uses job-order costing and applies overhead at 150% of direct labor cost. Job 101 used $12,000 of direct materials and 400 direct labor hours at $25 per hour, and produced 500 units. What is the unit cost of Job 101?
exp: Direct labor = 400 x $25 = $10,000; overhead = 150% x $10,000 = $15,000; total = $12,000 + $10,000 + $15,000 = $37,000, or $74 per unit. Applying the 150% rate to materials cost gives $80.

q: Quarry Co. uses weighted-average process costing; materials are added at the start of the process. Beginning work in process was 2,000 units (60% complete for conversion), 18,000 units were started, and ending work in process was 4,000 units (25% complete for conversion). What are the equivalent units for conversion costs?
exp: Units completed = 2,000 + 18,000 - 4,000 = 16,000; weighted-average conversion EU = 16,000 + (4,000 x 25%) = 17,000. The 15,800 figure is the FIFO calculation, which subtracts the 1,200 EU already in beginning inventory.

q: Rand Co. uses FIFO process costing. Beginning work in process was 5,000 units, 40% complete for conversion; 25,000 units were started; ending work in process was 3,000 units, 70% complete for conversion. What are Rand's equivalent units for conversion costs?
exp: FIFO EU = finish beginning WIP (5,000 x 60% = 3,000) + started and completed (22,000) + ending WIP (3,000 x 70% = 2,100) = 27,100. Using 40% for beginning WIP (work done last period) gives 26,100, and the weighted-average result is 29,100.

q: Stine Co. uses weighted-average process costing with materials added at the start. During the month 16,000 units were completed and 4,000 units remained in ending work in process, 50% complete for conversion. Total materials costs (beginning WIP plus current) were $100,000 and total conversion costs were $342,000. What cost is assigned to ending work in process?
exp: Materials EU = 20,000, so $5.00 per EU; conversion EU = 16,000 + 2,000 = 18,000, so $19.00 per EU; ending WIP = (4,000 x $5) + (2,000 x $19) = $58,000. Treating ending units as fully complete gives $96,000, and treating materials as only 50% added gives $48,000.

q: Thorne Co. incurs $120,000 of joint costs to produce 6,000 units of Product X, with a sales value at split-off of $20 per unit, and 4,000 units of Product Y, with a sales value at split-off of $45 per unit. Using the relative sales value at split-off method, how much joint cost is allocated to Product X?
exp: Sales values are $120,000 for X and $180,000 for Y, so X receives $120,000 / $300,000 x $120,000 = $48,000. Allocating on physical units (6,000 / 10,000) gives $72,000.

q: Upham Co. incurs $200,000 of joint costs. Product A can be sold only after further processing costing $60,000, for a final sales value of $300,000. Product B is sold at split-off for $160,000. Using the net realizable value method, how much joint cost is allocated to Product A?
exp: NRV of A = $300,000 - $60,000 = $240,000; NRV of B = $160,000; A's share = $240,000 / $400,000 x $200,000 = $120,000. Using A's final sales value without deducting separable costs gives $130,435.

q: Vail Co. produces 10,000 units of a joint product that can be sold at split-off for $30 per unit, or processed further at a cost of $8 per unit and sold for $36 per unit. Joint costs allocated to the product are $12 per unit. What should Vail do?
choices: Sell at split-off; processing further would reduce profit by $20,000
Sell at split-off; processing further would reduce profit by $140,000
exp: Incremental revenue of $6 per unit is less than the $8 incremental cost, so processing further lowers profit by $2 x 10,000 = $20,000. Joint costs are sunk at split-off and irrelevant; considering only the $6 revenue increase ignores the separable cost.

q: Wexler Co. makes 20,000 units of a component at a cost per unit of: direct materials $6, direct labor $8, variable overhead $4, and allocated fixed overhead $10. An outside supplier offers the component for $24 per unit. If Wexler buys, 40% of the fixed overhead would be eliminated. What should Wexler do?
exp: Relevant cost to make = $6 + $8 + $4 + ($10 x 40%) = $22, which is $2 below the $24 price, so making saves $2 x 20,000 = $40,000. Comparing full cost of $28 to $24 ($80,000 in favor of buying) wrongly includes unavoidable fixed overhead.

q: Yates Co. has capacity of 100,000 units and currently sells 80,000 units at $50. Variable cost is $30 per unit and fixed cost is $12 per unit at the current volume. A customer offers to buy 15,000 units at $36, requiring extra shipping of $2 per unit; regular sales are unaffected. What is the effect on operating income of accepting the order?
exp: With idle capacity, fixed costs are irrelevant: ($36 - $30 - $2) x 15,000 = $60,000 increase. Including the $12 fixed cost per unit produces a $120,000 decrease, a classic full-cost trap.

q: Zeller Co. has capacity of 100,000 units and sells 90,000 units at $50 with variable cost of $30. A customer offers to buy 20,000 units at $42 but will accept only the full quantity, so Zeller would have to give up 10,000 units of regular sales. What is the effect on operating income of accepting?
exp: Special-order CM = 20,000 x ($42 - $30) = $240,000; lost regular CM = 10,000 x ($50 - $30) = $200,000; net = $40,000 increase. Ignoring the displaced regular sales gives $240,000.

q: A segment of Amble Co. has sales of $500,000, variable costs of $350,000, direct fixed costs of $100,000 (of which $70,000 would be avoided if the segment were dropped), and allocated common fixed costs of $80,000. If Amble drops the segment, what is the effect on company operating income?
exp: Dropping loses $150,000 of contribution margin and saves $70,000 of avoidable fixed costs, a net decrease of $80,000. The segment's reported $30,000 loss includes unavoidable fixed and allocated common costs, so dropping it would not raise income.

q: Baird Co. began the year with no inventory, produced 50,000 units, and sold 45,000 units. Fixed manufacturing overhead was $400,000. How does operating income under absorption costing compare with operating income under variable costing?
exp: Fixed overhead per unit = $400,000 / 50,000 = $8; inventory rose 5,000 units, deferring $40,000 of fixed overhead under absorption costing, so absorption income is $40,000 higher. Using units sold as the denominator ($8.89 per unit) gives $44,444.

q: Cobb Co. reports per-unit costs of direct materials $10, direct labor $6, variable manufacturing overhead $4, fixed manufacturing overhead $5 (at normal capacity), and variable selling costs $3. What is the inventoriable cost per unit under variable costing?
exp: Variable costing inventories only variable manufacturing costs: $10 + $6 + $4 = $20. Adding variable selling costs ($23) is wrong because selling costs are never inventoriable, and $25 is the absorption cost.

q: Dunn Co. recorded maintenance costs and machine hours as follows: January, 4,000 hours and $30,000; February, 6,000 hours and $52,000; March, 9,000 hours and $50,000; April, 5,000 hours and $36,000. Using the high-low method, what are estimated maintenance costs at 7,000 machine hours?
exp: High-low uses the highest and lowest activity levels (March and January): variable rate = ($50,000 - $30,000) / (9,000 - 4,000) = $4 per hour; fixed = $50,000 - $36,000 = $14,000; estimate = $14,000 + $28,000 = $42,000. Selecting the highest-cost month (February) instead of the highest-activity month produces $63,000.

q: Egan Co. uses activity-based costing with these pools: setups $120,000 (300 setups), inspections $90,000 (1,500 inspections), and machining $300,000 (20,000 machine hours). Product Z required 40 setups, 200 inspections, and 2,000 machine hours to produce 1,000 units. What is Product Z's overhead cost per unit under ABC?
exp: Rates are $400 per setup, $60 per inspection, and $15 per machine hour: (40 x $400) + (200 x $60) + (2,000 x $15) = $58,000, or $58 per unit. A plantwide machine-hour rate ($510,000 / 20,000 = $25.50) would assign only $51 per unit.

q: Fryer Co.'s maintenance department costs of $60,000 are allocated based on usage: 20% to the IT service department, 50% to Production 1, and 30% to Production 2. Using the direct method, how much maintenance cost is allocated to Production 1?
exp: The direct method ignores service-to-service usage, so Production 1 receives 50 / (50 + 30) x $60,000 = $37,500. Applying the raw 50% ($30,000) fails to remove the IT department's share from the base.

q: Gill Co. has two service departments. Service A ($100,000) provides 20% of its services to Service B, 40% to Production 1, and 40% to Production 2. Service B ($60,000) provides 10% to Service A, 30% to Production 1, and 60% to Production 2. Using the step-down method and allocating Service A first, what total service cost is allocated to Production 1?
exp: A allocates $40,000 to P1 and $20,000 to B; B's $80,000 is then spread over the producing departments only: P1 gets 30/90 x $80,000 = $26,667, total $66,667. The direct method gives $70,000, and failing to renormalize B's percentages gives $64,000.

q: Hollis Co. started 10,000 units and finished 9,200 good units. Normal spoilage is 5% of good units produced, and the cost per unit is $50. What amount should Hollis recognize as a loss from abnormal spoilage?
exp: Total spoilage = 800 units; normal = 5% x 9,200 = 460; abnormal = 340 x $50 = $17,000, expensed as a period loss. Computing normal spoilage on units started (500) gives $15,000.

q: Inman Co.'s total costs are $340,000 at 20,000 units and $440,000 at 30,000 units, both within the relevant range. What is the expected total cost per unit at 25,000 units?
exp: Variable cost = $100,000 / 10,000 = $10 per unit; fixed = $340,000 - $200,000 = $140,000; total at 25,000 = $390,000, or $15.60 per unit. Averaging the two unit costs ($15.83) ignores that fixed costs spread differently at each volume.

q: Jett Co. incurred the following costs: factory rent $60,000, sales commissions $25,000, direct materials $150,000, direct labor $120,000, factory utilities $18,000, office salaries $70,000, factory supervisor salary $45,000, and advertising $30,000. Under absorption costing, what are Jett's total product costs?
exp: Product costs are manufacturing costs: $60,000 + $150,000 + $120,000 + $18,000 + $45,000 = $393,000. Sales commissions, office salaries, and advertising ($125,000) are period costs; including office salaries yields $463,000.

q: Kline Co. is pricing a special job that would use materials already in inventory. The materials originally cost $12,000 and would cost $15,000 to replace. Kline has no other use for them and could sell them as scrap for $3,000. What is the relevant cost of the materials for the job?
exp: Because the materials will not be replaced, the relevant cost is the opportunity cost of the forgone scrap proceeds, $3,000. Historical cost ($12,000) is sunk, and replacement cost matters only if the materials would be replaced.

q: Lowe Co. makes Product X (contribution margin $30, 3 machine hours per unit, demand 1,500 units) and Product Y (contribution margin $24, 2 machine hours per unit, demand 2,000 units). Only 6,000 machine hours are available. What is the maximum total contribution margin?
exp: CM per machine hour is $12 for Y and $10 for X, so produce all 2,000 Y (4,000 hours, $48,000) and use the remaining 2,000 hours on X ($20,000), for $68,000. Prioritizing X because it has the higher unit CM gives only $63,000.

q: Marsh Co. sold 40,000 units at $25 per unit. Variable manufacturing cost is $10 per unit and variable selling cost is $2 per unit. Fixed manufacturing overhead is $150,000 and fixed selling and administrative costs are $90,000. Marsh produced 50,000 units and had no beginning inventory. What is Marsh's operating income under absorption costing?
exp: Variable costing income = 40,000 x ($25 - $12) - $240,000 = $280,000; absorption defers fixed overhead of $3 per unit on 10,000 units ($30,000), so absorption income is $310,000. The $280,000 amount is variable costing income.

q: Department 2 of Nash Co. received 10,000 units from Department 1 and had no beginning inventory. Ending work in process is 2,000 units, 40% complete for conversion. Materials in Department 2 are added at the end of the process. Using the weighted-average method, what are the equivalent units for Department 2 materials?
exp: 8,000 units were completed and received materials; the 2,000 ending units have not reached the end of the process, so materials EU = 8,000. The 10,000 figure applies to transferred-in costs, and 8,800 is the conversion EU.

q: Orr Co. estimated overhead of $360,000 and 40,000 machine hours. Actual machine hours were 42,000 and actual overhead was $366,000. Unadjusted cost of goods sold is $500,000, and Orr closes any over- or underapplied overhead entirely to COGS. What is adjusted COGS?
exp: Rate = $9 per hour; applied = 42,000 x $9 = $378,000, which exceeds actual by $12,000 (overapplied), so COGS falls to $488,000. Adding the overapplied amount gives $512,000.

q: Pace Co. needs one production supervisor for each 5,000 units of monthly output or fraction thereof, at $40,000 per supervisor. Output is expected to increase from 12,000 to 16,000 units per month. What is the incremental supervision cost?
exp: This is a step cost: 12,000 units require 3 supervisors and 16,000 units require 4, so cost rises by $40,000. Treating the cost as variable ($8 per unit x 4,000 = $32,000) ignores its step behavior.

q: Quince Co. incurs $100,000 of joint costs producing main Products A and B and a by-product. The by-product's net realizable value of $10,000 is deducted from joint costs. A and B have relative sales values at split-off of 60% and 40%, respectively. How much joint cost is allocated to Product A?
exp: Net joint cost = $100,000 - $10,000 = $90,000; A's share = 60% x $90,000 = $54,000. Allocating the full $100,000 without the by-product credit gives $60,000.

q: Rios Co. applies overhead at 80% of direct labor cost. At year-end, Job 201 (direct materials $15,000, direct labor $10,000) has been completed and sold, Job 202 (direct materials $9,000, direct labor $12,000) is completed but unsold, and Job 203 (direct materials $8,000, direct labor $6,000) is in process. What is the ending finished goods inventory?
exp: Only Job 202 is in finished goods: $9,000 + $12,000 + (80% x $12,000) = $30,600. Omitting applied overhead gives $21,000; Job 203 ($18,800) is work in process and Job 201 ($33,000) is in COGS.

q: Sloan Co. must sell a new product at the market price of $120 and wants a profit equal to 25% of the selling price. The current estimated cost is $96 per unit. Using target costing, how much must Sloan reduce unit cost?
exp: Target cost = $120 - (25% x $120) = $90, so cost must fall by $96 - $90 = $6. Treating 25% as a markup on cost ($120 / 1.25 = $96) wrongly suggests no reduction is needed.

q: A product line of Tracy Co. generates contribution margin of $80,000 and incurs $20,000 of avoidable fixed costs. If the line is dropped, its factory space could be rented to another company for $50,000 per year. What should Tracy do?
exp: Keeping yields $80,000 - $20,000 = $60,000; dropping and renting yields $50,000, so keeping is $10,000 better. Ignoring the rental income (the opportunity cost of the space) overstates keeping's advantage at $60,000.

q: Umber Co. uses FIFO process costing with materials added at the start. Beginning WIP of 5,000 units (40% complete for conversion) carried costs of $62,000. During the period 25,000 units were started, and ending WIP was 3,000 units (70% complete). Current-period costs were $300,000 for materials and $271,000 for conversion. What is the cost of units completed and transferred out?
exp: FIFO EU: materials 25,000 ($12.00), conversion 3,000 + 22,000 + 2,100 = 27,100 ($10.00). Transferred out = $62,000 + (3,000 x $10) + 22,000 x $22 = $576,000. Omitting the cost to finish beginning WIP yields $546,000.

q: Vick Co. has two service departments. S1 ($40,000) provides 25% of its services to S2; S2 ($30,000) provides 20% of its services to S1. Using the reciprocal method, what is S1's total reciprocal cost to be allocated?
exp: S1 = 40,000 + 0.20 S2 and S2 = 30,000 + 0.25 S1, so S1 = 46,000 + 0.05 S1 and S1 = $46,000 / 0.95 = $48,421. Stopping after one round ($46,000) ignores the reciprocal service S1 receives back.

q: Wade Co. adds materials when units are 60% complete. During the month 9,000 units were completed and 2,000 units remained in ending work in process, 30% complete for conversion. There was no beginning inventory. What are the equivalent units for materials?
exp: Ending WIP at 30% has not reached the 60% point where materials are added, so materials EU = 9,000 completed units only. Counting ending units as receiving materials gives 11,000.

q: Xavier Co. is considering replacing a machine with a book value of $40,000 that can be sold now for $10,000. A new machine costs $60,000 and would cut cash operating costs by $15,000 per year over its 4-year life; neither machine has salvage value at the end. Ignoring income taxes and the time value of money, what is the net advantage or disadvantage of replacing?
exp: Relevant flows: savings $60,000 + sale proceeds $10,000 - new machine $60,000 = $10,000 advantage for replacing. The old machine's $40,000 book value is sunk; deducting it produces the misleading $30,000 advantage for keeping.
